item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 14 - September 21, 2026
item.description:
QE ArXiv Watch Weekly — Week ending Sep 21, 2026 (4 papers)

If you’ve ever tried to “validate” a gen‑AI workflow with the same instincts you use for gage R&R or reliability growth, this week has a satisfying theme: stop treating evaluation as a leaderboard exercise and start treating it as an evidence-and-uncertainty problem. That shows up in enterprise LLM rollouts, medical forecasting, and rare-event probability estimation.

When “it looks good” isn’t decision-grade: enterprise GenAI gets a reliability-style eval frame

Ali et al.’s EnterpriseVal is the closest thing I’ve seen to an attempt at bringing engineering qualification thinking to enterprise generative AI. The move I like: the “evaluation object” isn’t a model—it’s a frozen socio-technical configuration (model + prompts + retrieval/tools + guardrails + human review) tied to a specific use case and local ground truth. That’s exactly how these systems fail in practice.

They also introduce an autonomy × consequence matrix to scale evaluation intensity. That’s basically a risk-based control plan for AI.

Where it gets very QE-friendly is the metric set: not just “accuracy,” but things like pass^k across repeated runs (stability), reviewer catch rate and false acceptance (oversight effectiveness), and explicit time/cost per successful task (value). The grading protocol—blinded experts plus LLM-as-judge corrected with prediction-powered inference—aims at making human evaluation cheaper without pretending it’s free.

Skeptical note: their pilot numbers (e.g., citation precision 88%, hallucination rate 1.6% in a credit memo workflow; big estimated hours saved in procedure transformation) are intriguing, but they themselves admit the uncomfortable part: no sample sizes, CIs, inter-rater agreement, or repeated-run rigor were recorded. So treat it as a strong framework with an illustrative pilot—not yet a qualification report.

Sparse longitudinal forecasting: accuracy is easy; reliable intervals are the real product

Kong et al. build a carefully QC’d benchmark for lesion-size forecasting with sparse CT follow-ups—five visits per trajectory, patient-level splits, and a fixed horizon design (predicting the same visit-to-visit change). That design choice matters: it prevents “easy horizons” from masquerading as model skill.

Two practitioner takeaways:

1. Most of the value is in the most recent extra observation. RMSE improves from m=1 to m=2, then flattens (and even worsens slightly). If you’re designing a monitoring schedule, that’s the kind of result you can act on.

2. Interval reliability isn’t the same as probabilistic calibration. Methods had near-perfect raw 95% coverage (some essentially 1.00), but PIT errors and NLL still varied. Conformal calibration helps coverage, but it doesn’t magically make the distribution “right.” If you’re using forecasts to trigger interventions, you want both coverage and sensible sharpness/likelihood behavior.

Also worth noting: their Gompertz-inspired regularizer mostly didn’t help; CV picked λ=0. A nice reminder that “biologically inspired” constraints can become accuracy taxes.

Rare-event reliability: importance sampling meets flows, with a “don’t collapse” mechanism

Helal et al. push adaptive importance sampling using mixtures of normalizing flows (FAMIS) for tiny failure probabilities. The clever bit is engineering around what usually breaks these methods: multimodal failure regions and mode collapse.

They combine (i) a defensive heavy-tailed exploration component (good early coverage), (ii) an annealed surrogate for the failure indicator (so you can learn without seeing failures), and (iii) a repulsion term (JSD) to keep mixture components from piling onto one mode. Reported results show stability and accuracy even into high dimensions where some baselines degrade, with a predictable evaluation budget N_{call}=KT+K_{est}. If you’re spending money on limit-state calls, that budget predictability is a feature, not a footnote.

A “reliability” paper that’s really about label noise (still useful)

Akhtar et al.’s Barge isn’t reliability-of-systems, but it is about reliability of supervision: imbalanced classification under noisy labels. The bounded, redescending loss is the practical idea—when a label looks confidently wrong, it stops dominating training. If you’ve got inspection labels, field-return codes, or human dispositions with known contamination, that’s directly relevant.

What to ponder this week

Across domains, the trend is the same: we’re moving from point performance to decision reliability—repeatability, calibrated uncertainty, oversight effectiveness, and cost-to-evidence. The open question for us: What’s the gen‑AI equivalent of an MSA report with confidence bounds and ongoing stability monitoring—and who in the org owns it?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Ali et al.: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise (Reliability)
  • Kong et al.: Reliability-Centered Evaluation of Sparse Longitudinal CT Lesion-Size Forecasting with Conformal Interval Calibration and Gompertz-Inspired Regularization (Reliability)
  • Helal et al.: Repulsive normalizing flow mixtures for adaptive importance sampling: reliability analysis of complex systems (Reliability)
  • Akhtar et al.: Bounded Adjustment with Reliability-Guided Embedding for Imbalanced Learning with Noisy Labels (Reliability)
